newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Start of Q1 earnings, PPI data.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Start of Q1 earnings, PPI data.

text.p: First quarter earnings will begin to exert their hold over Wall Street this week, starting with Motorola Inc's report after Monday's stock market close.
In addition to the flow of earnings, the market will focus on Friday's March producer price index and retail sales for further hints as to when the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again.

On-target or better-than-forecast earnings from Motorola will give the high-technology sector, which late last week rebounded from a sharp sell-off and saw the return of some momentum players, a further boost.
But the real test will come with International Business Machines Corp, Intel Corp and Microsoft Corp, due out later in the period, analysts said.

"Bad news from Motorola will have a short-term negative effect. But any good news will help the techs rally," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "The market is oversold and looking for good news."

Analysts said they were hoping for a reflex rally this week after the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 214.52 points last week, the fourth-largest weekly point loss in New York Stock Exchange history. The Dow staged a rebound rally on Friday, closing up 48.72 points at 6526.07.

"We could have a reflex oversold rally that will last all week long and can take us back to 6600," said Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "I think we are oversold enough for people to be convinced that prices are pretty low and there is a playable rally here."
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, said that it looked as though, for the time being, the correction in small-cap stocks was over.

"That is encouraging to see. If we get any relief for the large caps, we could stage a meaningful rally," he said. He said that Friday's PPI would be closely watched, but not as closely as last Friday's March employment report.

"Everything will be closely watched. You can't get away from that," Johnson said. "Inflation is a concern, but not as much as wage pressures and hourly earnings. We are seeing upward pressure on wages, but it has not gone through to producer and consumer prices."

Producer prices are expected to come in unchanged in March after having dropped 0.4 percent in February, according to a Reuter survey of U.S. economists. The core rate, which excludes food and energy, is expected to increase by 0.1 percent, compared to 0.1 percent drop the previous month.

Retail sales are expected to increase 0.6 percent in March compared to a 0.8 percent increase in February. The core rate, which excludes autos, is expected to increase by 0.4 percent, compared to 0.5 percent increase in February.
